q: 201. Ruling gradient on hill roads 300 m above M.S.L. is kept
explain: For hill roads at lower altitudes (up to 3000m), the ruling gradient is typically kept at 5% (1 in 20) to ensure vehicles can climb without excessive engine strain.

q: 202. If the radius of curvature of a hill road is 50 m, the percentage grade compensation should be
explain: IRC recommends grade compensation as 75/R percent, subject to a maximum of 4% total compensation.

q: 203. If N is the algebraic difference of grades, S is the minimum sight distance in metres, the length (L) of a summit curve is
explain: When L > S, the length of a summit curve for stopping sight distance is calculated as L = NS²/4.4 (often simplified to NS²/4 in older textbooks).

q: 204. If N is the net difference of grades, S is the minimum overtaken sight distance in metres, the length (L) of a summit curve, is
explain: For Overtaking Sight Distance (OSD), the height of the eye and object are both taken as 1.2m, leading to the formula L = NS²/9.6.

q: 205. For night travel, the length of a valley curve should be such that the head light beam distance is the same as
explain: Valley curves are designed based on 'Headlight Sight Distance,' which must be at least equal to the Stopping Sight Distance (SSD) for safety at night.

q: 206. The minimum vertical clearance of overhanging cliffs or any other structure above the surface of a hill road, should be
explain: A standard vertical clearance of 5 meters is maintained to accommodate high-body trucks and emergency vehicles on mountain roads.

q: 207. A gradient along which the vehicle does not require any tractive effort to maintain a specified speed, is known as
explain: A floating gradient is one where the resistance to motion is exactly balanced by the descending component of the vehicle's weight.

q: 208. Formation width of a hill road is the distance between
options: outer end of side drain to outer end of parapet wall
outer end of side drain to inner end of parapet wall
inner end of side drain to outer end of parapet wall
inner end of side drain to inner end of parapet wall
explain: In hill roads, the formation width is measured from the inner edge of the side drain to the outer edge of the parapet wall/retaining wall.

q: 209. Normal formation width of a hill road for one-way traffic, is
explain: The standard formation width for a single-lane hill road (one-way traffic) is approximately 4.8 meters.

q: 210. The wall constructed for the stability of an excavated portion of a road on the hill side, is known as
explain: Breast walls are specifically used to support the soil on the uphill side (cut side) of the road.

q: 211. The wall constructed for the stability of a filling portion of a road on the downhill side, is known as
explain: Retaining walls are built on the downhill side (valley side) to support the road embankment filling.

q: 212. Retaining walls are generally constructed with dry rubble stones with 60 cm top width and
explain: A front batter of 1:4 (1 horizontal to 4 vertical) is common for dry rubble masonry retaining walls to ensure stability.

q: 213. In retaining and breast walls, weep holes are provided at
options: 50 cm vertical height and 50 cm c/c horizontally
100 cm vertical height and 100 cm c/c horizontally
100 cm vertical height and 120 cm c/c horizontally
120 cm vertical height and 100 cm c/c horizontally
explain: Weep holes are placed at roughly 1-meter intervals (100 cm) both ways to drain water and prevent hydrostatic pressure build-up.

q: 214. Along a hill road, a side drain is provided on
options: outer side of a spur curve
outer side of a re-entrant curve
explain: Water is always directed toward the hill-side (inner side) to prevent it from washing over the embankment edge and causing erosion.

q: 215. Parapet walls along hill roads, are provided
options: to prevent the hill from sliding
to prevent the wheels of the vehicle from coming on the retaining wall
explain: Parapet walls serve as a safety barrier to keep vehicles from running off the edge of the road or onto the top of the retaining wall.

q: 216. Hill roads are
explain: In many hill road designs, cross-slope is provided as a single inward slope (super-elevation) toward the drain rather than a bidirectional camber.

q: 217. Intermediate catch water drains are provided only, if
options: catchment area of the watershed above road is large
single catch water drain is inadequate
explain: Catch water drains prevent surface runoff from the hill above from reaching the road; multiple drains are needed if the volume is too high for one.

q: 218. Side drains on both sides of a hill road, are essential when the road is
explain: When a road is in a full cutting, water enters from both slopes, necessitating drains on both sides of the pavement.

q: 219. Stability of hill slopes depends upon
explain: Stability is determined by the internal friction of the soil (nature), the steepness (angle), and the presence of rock bedding planes (geology).

q: 220. An ideal pavement is constructed with
explain: Portland Cement Concrete (PCC) is considered ideal for high-durability, long-life pavements with low tractive resistance.

q: 221. In case of cement concrete pavements, pick up the incorrect statement
options: initial cost of construction is high
initial cost of construction is low
explain: Concrete pavements are known for having a high initial construction cost compared to flexible (bituminous) pavements.

q: 222. The basic formula for determination of pavement thickness was first suggested by
explain: Goldbeck provided early simplified formulas for pavement thickness based on wheel loads and allowable stresses.

q: 223. When each particle of aggregates is thinly coated with cement paste, a heterogeneous solid is formed, which is known as
explain: Concrete is a composite material formed by binding aggregates (sand/gravel) together with cement paste.

q: 224. For maximum strength and durability minimum percentage of cement, by weight is
explain: Standard mixes like 1:2:4 or M20 roughly result in a cement content around 15% by weight of the total mix.

q: 225. To indicate proper control of consistency of a freshly mixed concrete for pavement construction, the slump should be between
explain: Road concrete requires a very stiff mix (low workability) to ensure high strength and prevent flow; hence a low slump of 3-5 cm is used.

q: 226. The formula for calculating the depth of concrete pavements suggested by Goldbeck, is
explain: Goldbeck's formula for corner loading is d = √(3W/σ), where W is the wheel load and σ is the allowable stress.

q: 227. When load is applied on concrete pavement
options: away from edges, the maximum bending moment is negative
away from edges, the maximum bending moment cause compression
on the edges, the maximum stress is parallel to the edge
explain: Interior loading (away from edges) causes the slab to deflect like a dish, creating negative bending moments and tension at the bottom.

q: 228. For the design of cement concrete pavement for corner loading, Indian Road Congress recommends the use of
explain: While Westergaard is more theoretically complex, IRC historically used simplified versions like Goldbeck's for practical corner design.

q: 229. If d is the economic designed depth of a slab, the thickness of the cement concrete pavement slab at interior, is kept
explain: The interior of the slab experiences less stress than the corners/edges, so the thickness can be reduced to roughly 85% of the edge thickness.

q: 230. Reinforcement in cement concrete slab of road pavements, is placed
options: in the form of welded wire mesh
explain: Reinforcement is provided in both directions to control temperature cracks and distribute loads efficiently.

q: 231. Depth of reinforcement below the surface of a concrete pavement, is generally kept
explain: A standard cover of 5 cm is maintained to protect the steel from corrosion while remaining effective in resisting surface-level stresses.

q: 232. To prevent compressive stresses in a rigid concrete pavement, the joint provided, is
explain: Expansion joints allow the slab to lengthen during hot weather, preventing compressive buckling.

q: 233. Transverse joints are provided at distances varying from
explain: Modern spacing for expansion joints in rigid pavements typically falls in the 17m to 27m range, depending on temperature variation.

q: 234. Minimum thickness of a layer of fine sand required to cut off capillary rise of water completely, should be
explain: To completely break the capillary attraction in fine-grained soils, a thick sand blanket of about 76 cm is required.

q: 235. To prevent movement of moisture from subgrade to road pavement at the same level as that of water-table, thickness of a cut off layer of coarse sand, is
explain: Coarse sand has larger voids, making a thinner layer (15 cm) effective as a capillary cut-off compared to fine sand.

q: 236. Newly constructed pavement with ordinary Portland cement attains its working strength after
explain: Concrete is traditionally considered to have reached its full design strength at the 28-day curing mark.

q: 237. Pavement is said to be flexible if it contains
explain: Flexible pavements are those that deform under load and transmit pressure through grain-to-grain contact; WBM and bitumen layers fit this description.

q: 238. Design of flexible pavement, involves
explain: Designers must consider the magnitude of load, frequency of application (traffic), and environmental factors like rainfall and temperature.

q: 239. Design of flexible pavements is based on
options: a compromise of pure theory and empirical formula
explain: Most flexible pavement design methods (like CBR) are based on empirical observations and testing rather than rigid structural theory.

q: 240. California Bearing Ratio method of designing flexible pavements is more accurate as it involves
options: character of the road making materials
explain: The CBR test directly measures the resistance of the subgrade soil to penetration, which is the primary factor in flexible pavement thickness.

q: 241. Bottom-most component of a flexible pavement, is
explain: The subgrade is the prepared natural soil foundation upon which all other layers are built.

q: 242. Cement grouted pavement is classified as
explain: Because it uses a cement binder within a stone matrix but doesn't have the full structural slab action of PCC, it is called semi-rigid.

q: 243. Thickness of a pavement may be reduced considerably by
options: combination of all of the above
explain: Improving the strength of the subgrade through any of these methods allows for a thinner (and cheaper) upper pavement structure.

q: 244. Minimum thickness of the base of a flexible pavement is
explain: A standard minimum of 10 cm is required for the base layer to ensure proper load distribution and construction stability.

q: 245. For a poorly graded sub-grade soil, thickness of sub-base, is
explain: Poorly graded soils have low bearing capacity, requiring a thick sub-base layer (30 cm) to protect the subgrade.

q: 246. Traffic engineering only includes
options: design and application of control devices
explain: Traffic engineering is a broad field covering the safe and efficient movement of people and goods through planning, design, and operations.

q: 247. For clear distinct vision, images of obstructions should fall on the retina with a cone of
explain: Acute vision is limited to a small central field of view, generally cited as a 3-degree cone in traffic psychology.

q: 248. In complex situations, total time required for a driver to form a judgment and to act, may be taken as
explain: While standard reaction is 2.5s, complex urban or hazardous situations may require up to 3.0 seconds for full processing.

q: 249. Design of highways is based on
explain: Pavement structural design is primarily governed by the weight transmitted through the axle loads (e.g., the 8160 kg standard axle).

q: 250. Width of vehicles affects the width of
explain: The physical width of a vehicle (standard 2.44m or 2.5m) directly dictates the necessary width of the traffic lane (standard 3.5m or 3.75m).

q: 251. Length of vehicles does not affect
explain: The width of shoulders is determined by the need for emergency parking and lateral support, whereas vehicle length is a critical factor for off-tracking (widening) and sight distances.

q: 252. The weight of vehicles affects
explain: Pavement thickness is structurally designed based on the magnitude of wheel loads and axle weights to prevent fatigue and rutting.

q: 253. Design of horizontal and vertical alignments, super-elevation, sight distance and grades, is worst affected by
explain: Speed is the most dominant variable in geometric design; it dictates the required radius of curves, the rate of super-elevation, and the necessary stopping distance.

q: 254. Speed regulations on roads is decided on the basis of
explain: The 85th percentile speed is a standard traffic engineering metric representing the speed at or below which 85% of motorists drive; it is considered a safe and reasonable speed limit.

q: 255. Minimum permissible speed on high speed roads, is decided on the basis of
explain: The 15th percentile speed is used to set the lower speed limit to prevent slow-moving vehicles from creating hazards or bottlenecks.

q: 256. On most smooth hard surfaced roads, rolling resistance to moving vehicles, ranges from
explain: For standard hard pavements, the rolling resistance typically falls within the 9 to 11 kg per tonne range.

q: 257. Gradient resistance of moving vehicles along down slopes, is
explain: On a down slope, gravity assists the movement, effectively acting as a negative resistance (roughly 10 kg/tonne for every 1% of grade; here 9 kg/tonne is the closest technical value).

q: 258. The maximum comfortable retardation applied to moving vehicles, is
explain: A deceleration rate of 3.4 m/s² is generally considered the threshold for passenger comfort during braking.

q: 259. The distance travelled by revolving the wheel of a vehicle more than its circumferential movement, is known as
explain: Slip occurs when the wheel rotates more than the actual distance covered (common during acceleration on slippery surfaces).

q: 260. Along horizontal curves, if centrifugal force exceeds lateral friction, vehicles may
explain: A skid occurs when the tires lose traction and the vehicle slides laterally because the outward centrifugal force is higher than the sideways resistance.

q: 261. Driving vehicles on wet surfaced roads, is dangerous because it may
explain: Water acts as a lubricant, significantly reducing the coefficient of friction and increasing the risk of skidding (hydroplaning).

q: 262. Roughness index of roads, is expressed as
options: size of the stone on the pavement
number of patches on the pavement
cumulative deformation of surface per horizontal distance
explain: The Roughness Index (measured by a bump integrator) is the sum of vertical undulations per unit length of road (mm/km).

q: 263. Traffic surveys are carried out
options: to know the type of traffic
to determine the facilities to traffic regulations
explain: Surveys provide data for every aspect of highway design, from structural capacity (traffic types) to geometric safety and auxiliary systems.

q: 264. Traffic census is carried out for
explain: A comprehensive traffic census captures volume, speed, and parking patterns to understand the overall demand on the infrastructure.

q: 265. At intersection of roads, the traffic volume study is carried out to ascertain the number of vehicles
explain: Directional counts are essential at intersections to design signal timings and dedicated turning lanes.

q: 266. Increase in traffic volume, due to increase in transport vehicles, is known as
explain: Normal growth accounts for the general increase in vehicle ownership and population over time, independent of a specific new road project.

q: 267. Volume of traffic which is due to improvement carried out in adjacent area, is known as
explain: Development traffic is the additional traffic generated by new land uses (like a new mall or residential colony) near the highway.

q: 268. Volume of traffic which would immediately use a new road or an improved one when opened to traffic, is known
explain: Current traffic is the initial volume expected on day one, consisting of existing traffic diverted from other routes.

q: 269. Maximum number of passenger cars that can pass a given point on a road during one hour under the most ideal road way and traffic conditions, is known as
explain: Basic capacity is the theoretical maximum under 'ideal' conditions, assuming all vehicles travel at the same speed and minimum spacing.

q: 270. Maximum number of vehicles that can pass a given point on a lane during one hour without creating un-reasonable delay, is known as
explain: Practical capacity (or design capacity) is the volume that can be handled while maintaining a specific Level of Service (LOS) and acceptable delay.

q: 271. Customers prefer parking of their vehicles at
explain: 90-degree parking is the most space-efficient and common preference for commercial parking lots and aisles.

q: 272. If brakes of vehicles are effective, the vehicle-running at 30 km/hour comes to a stop in
explain: Under standard braking conditions for a speed of 30 km/h, the average stopping distance required is approximately 10 meters.

q: 273. The head light of vehicles should be such that its lower beam illuminates objects at
explain: For safety, the dipped (lower) beam should reach at least 30 meters to provide sufficient reaction time at low urban speeds.

q: 274. In case of a multi-lane road, overtaking is generally permitted
options: from both sides right and left
explain: In countries that drive on the left (like Nepal/India), overtaking is legally performed from the right side for better visibility of oncoming traffic.

q: 275. One-way streets are generally provided in crowded cities as, these
options: are inexpensive means of traffic flow
explain: One-way systems eliminate head-on conflicts, simplify signal timing, and generally improve flow and safety in dense grids.

q: 276. At a road junction, 16 cross conflict points are severe, if
options: one is two-way road and other is one-way road
explain: A standard intersection of two two-way roads creates 24 conflict points, 16 of which are major 'crossing' conflicts.

q: 277. At a road junction, 7 cross conflict points are severe if
options: one is two-way road and other is one-way road
explain: Reducing one of the roads to one-way traffic significantly drops the number of severe crossing conflict points (to approximately 7).

q: 278. To prevent a head-on-collision of vehicles travelling in opposite directions along four-lane roads
options: marking on the road are provided
medians of wide area are provided
explain: Physical dividers (medians) are the most effective way to eliminate the possibility of vehicles crossing into oncoming traffic.

q: 279. Longitudinal pavement lines marked broken in white paint
options: are for the guidance of the drivers
are not to be crossed over
may be crossed over at the discretion of the driver
explain: Broken white lines indicate that lane changing or overtaking is permitted when safe; solid lines indicate crossing is prohibited.

q: 280. Road makers along roads from the edge of a kerb should not be less than
explain: A minimum lateral clearance of 60 cm is maintained from the kerb to any vertical signpost or marker to avoid being struck by vehicle mirrors.

q: 281. From the point of tangency before an intersection, the route markers are fixed at a distance of
explain: Advanced route markers are placed well ahead of the intersection (100–150m) to give drivers time to change lanes safely.

q: 282. Along high ways confirmatory route markers are generally fixed
options: before the crossing on the left side
after the crossing on the left side
before the crossing on the right side
after the crossing on the right side
explain: Confirmatory markers are placed after an intersection to reassure the driver they are on the correct route.

q: 283. The top height of a route marker above crown level is
explain: A standard height of 1.75 meters ensures the sign is within the driver's line of sight without being obscured by low-hanging foliage.

q: 284. Thickness of broken centre line markings for a four lane road, is generally kept
explain: Standard lane line thickness is 15 cm to ensure high visibility at highway speeds.

q: 285. Thickness of broken line markings on multi-lane road for lanes is generally kept
explain: Individual lane dividers within a multi-lane road are sometimes kept slightly thinner (10 cm) than the main center line.

q: 286. Passing zones are generally not provided on
explain: Passing is restricted anywhere visibility is limited (curves/summits) or where the road is too narrow to permit safe overtaking.

q: 287. Round-about are not suitable if number of vehicles exceed
explain: Conventional roundabouts lose efficiency when total entering traffic exceeds 3000 vehicles per hour, leading to excessive weaving delays.

q: 288. Width of a rotary round should be equal to
options: twice the width of narrowest radial road
width of the widest road plus the width of one lane
width of the widest road plus 2 metres
explain: The circulatory roadway width is designed based on the widest entering road to ensure capacity is not throttled within the rotary.

q: 289. The weaving length of a roadway is the distance
options: equal to total width of adjoining radial roads
explain: Weaving length is the distance between two adjacent channelizing islands where vehicles crossing paths must merge and diverge.

q: 290. For the movement of vehicles at an intersection of two roads, without any interference, the type of grade separator generally preferred to, is
explain: The full cloverleaf interchange allows for all possible turns between two crossing highways without any traffic signals or crossing conflicts.

q: 291. A subsidiary area in a carriageway placed so as to control the movement of the traffic, is
explain: Traffic islands are raised or painted areas used to channelize vehicles and protect pedestrians.

q: 292. If cross slope of a country is upto 10% the terrain is classified as
explain: According to IRC classifications, terrain with a cross-slope of 0-10% is 'Plain'.

q: 293. If cross slope of a country is 10% to 25%, the terrain is classified as
explain: Terrain with a cross-slope of 10-25% is classified as 'Rolling'.

q: 294. If the cross slope of a country is 25% to 60%, the terrain is classified as
explain: Terrain with a cross-slope of 25-60% is classified as 'Mountainous'.

q: 295. If cross slope of a country is greater than 60%, the terrain is classified as
explain: Terrain with a cross-slope exceeding 60% is classified as 'Steep'.

q: 296. The minimum design speed of various types of highways in plain terrain is the same as the ruling design speed of
explain: The minimum speed requirement for a higher-tier terrain (plain) often aligns with the ruling (standard) speed of the next most difficult tier (rolling).

q: 297. Set-back distance is the distance between
options: road land boundary and building line
road land boundary and control line
road land boundary and control line
explain: The set-back distance ensures that no permanent structures are built too close to the road boundary for safety and future expansion.

q: 298. A single lane carriage way whenever changes to two-lane carriage way, is affected through a tape of
explain: A taper ratio between 1:15 and 1:20 is required to transition the road width smoothly without surprising the driver.

q: 299. The desirable camber for straight roads with water bound macadam or gravel surface, is
explain: WBM surfaces are more porous and rough, requiring a steeper camber (3% to 4%) for effective drainage.

q: 300. The desirable camber for straight roads with thin bituminous surfacing, is
explain: For thin bituminous layers, a camber of 2.5% to 3% (1 in 40 to 1 in 33) is the standard requirement.
